Cologne
kuh-LOHN
n. (the great Rhineland archbishopric, where Hermann von Wied's attempted Reformation was crushed in 1546)
From Latin Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium, shortened to Colonia; German Köln, French Cologne.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Cologne was the largest city in Germany through the Middle Ages, an archbishopric whose holder was one of the seven electors, and the most determinedly conservative church centre in the empire; its university condemned Luther in 1519, Tyndale's first printing of the English New Testament was broken up there in 1525, and its relics of the Three Kings drew pilgrims from all Europe to a cathedral that stood unfinished with a crane on its stump for three hundred years. Against that background Hermann von Wied, archbishop from 1515, grew convinced of the Reformation, brought in Bucer and Melanchthon in 1542 to draft a reforming order for his province, and was excommunicated and deposed by 1547, his clergy and university having fought him throughout. The dictionary records Cologne for the resistance rather than the attempt. Paul warned the Ephesian elders that the opposition would rise from inside the ministry itself, and he foretold a time when men would not endure sound doctrine but would prefer teachers chosen to suit them.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines sound as whole and uncorrupted; doctrine as that which is taught; to endure as to bear with patience; perverse as obstinately wrong; and a teacher as one who instructs.

expand to see more

SOUND, a. Entire; unbroken; not shaky or decayed; healthy; founded in truth; firm; valid; orthodox.

DOCTRINE, n. Whatever is taught; principles or positions in any science; the truths of the gospel in general.

ENDURE, v.t. To bear; to sustain; to support without breaking or yielding; to undergo; to tolerate.

PERVERSE, a. Literally, turned aside; hence, distorted from the right; obstinate in the wrong; stubborn.

TEACHER, n. One who teaches or instructs; an instructor; a preceptor; one who instructs others in religion.

Key Scripture

Act 20:30 — "Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them."

2Ti 4:3 — "For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears;"

Tit 1:9 — "Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers."

1Jo 4:1 — "Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world."

Modern Corruption

Largest German city and an electoral archbishopric, whose clergy and university defeated Archbishop Hermann von Wied's attempted Reformation by 1547.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Paul's warning about the source of the worst opposition, which is not outside the church: “Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them” (Act 20:30). He describes the appetite that makes such men successful, that the time will come “when they will not endure sound doctrine” (2Ti 4:3).

The live temptation at Cologne was a prosperous religion with everything to lose, a cathedral full of relics, a university with a reputation, and a clergy with incomes, all of it mobilised against its own archbishop. The qualification Paul requires of an overseer is competence in the deposit rather than in the politics: “Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught” (Tit 1:9). And the duty of testing falls on ordinary believers as well: “believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God” (1Jo 4:1). Hermann von Wied was deposed; the New Testament he could not stop printing was printed in Worms.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek diastrepho (G1294), to distort; Greek hugiaino (G5198), to be sound or healthy; Greek antecho (G0472), to hold fast; Greek dokimazo (G1381), to test.

expand to see more

Greek diastrepho (G1294) — to distort, to pervert; “speaking perverse things”, Acts 20:30.

Greek apospao (G0645) — to draw away, to drag off; “to draw away disciples after them”, Acts 20:30.

Greek hugiaino (G5198) — to be healthy, to be sound; “they will not endure sound doctrine”, 2 Timothy 4:3.

Greek antecho (G0472) — to hold firmly to; “Holding fast the faithful word”, Titus 1:9.

Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to test, to prove; “try the spirits whether they are of God”, 1 John 4:1.

Usage

"“Also of your own selves shall men arise” (Act 20:30) — where the resistance came from."

"“they will not endure sound doctrine” (2Ti 4:3) — the appetite that defeated an archbishop."

"“Holding fast the faithful word” (Tit 1:9) — the qualification that was missing."
